Co-driving Indonesia

Can VinFast turn co-creation into its Asian growth engine? A strategic review of VinFast Indonesia's "Your Voice, Our Future" campaign (2025).

Minh Hieu Ong · 104680710 · MKT30016Published page: [link]

Figure 1. Co-driving Indonesia (author's design).

1The campaign

On 7 October 2025, VinFast Indonesia launched "Your Voice, Our Future" (Suaramu Penentu Langkah Kami), a nationwide vote on future designs for the VF 5, VF 6, VF 7, VF 8 and VF 9. Indonesians could choose their favourite exterior and interior concepts online or at malls and showrooms, upload their own sketches, and compete for a prize pool of IDR 1.335 billion. Voting closed on 18 October and winners were named on 26 October (VinFast Indonesia, 2025a).

2First impression

What stopped me was the confidence of it. A Vietnamese newcomer, selling against BYD, Wuling and Chery, handed part of its design process to the public. VinFast is a challenger here: its best seller, the VF e34, ranked sixth in Indonesia's 2025 electric car wholesales, behind five Chinese models (KatadataOTO, 2026). The timing matters too. In April 2025 VinFast paused expansion in Western markets to focus on Asia (Viet Nam News, 2025b), so this campaign is a test of how the brand plans to win in its new priority region.

Two questions shaped my review. Can co-creation become a repeatable way to enter Asian markets? And is the campaign's "green transformation" message backed by anything a customer could measure?

3Segmentation, targeting and positioning

VinFast does not publish its segments, so I inferred them from its range and messaging. Its line-up runs from the VF 3 city car at Rp195 million to the VF 7 SUV at Rp499 million (Liputan6, 2025; Viet Nam News, 2025a). That points to demographic segmentation by income and life stage, plus a behavioural split between first-time EV buyers and drivers switching from petrol cars. The campaign itself, however, invited "Indonesian consumers and citizens in general" to vote (VinFast Indonesia, 2025a). In Kotler et al.'s (2023) terms, a differentiated product line was promoted with an almost undifferentiated campaign.

That choice buys reach, not necessarily buyers. Anyone can vote, including people with no plan to buy an EV, and the campaign left out the VF 3, VinFast's entry model. Sales data suggests conversion is the real problem. Herawati (2025) reported that only 2,628 of 15,168 imported VinFast units had reached retail customers, around 17 percent, and detikOto (2025b) put VinFast at 3.78 percent of Indonesia's EV sales for January to November 2025.

The positioning is clearer and smarter. BYD's Atto 1 matches the VF 3 at Rp195 million (Suara, 2025), so a price fight is hard to win. Instead, VinFast positions on voice, local identity and long-term assurance, backed by warranties of up to 10 years and free charging until 2028 (Viet Nam News, 2025a). This is co-creation in Prahalad and Ramaswamy's (2004) sense: value built with customers rather than for them. Figure 2 shows the space this leaves VinFast to own.

For international expansion, co-creation is portable because it is cheap to run and signals respect for local taste. The risk is expectation. VinFast only says winning ideas "may" inspire future models (VinFast Indonesia, 2025a). If nothing visible follows, participants learn that their voice was a marketing device.

4Social media and digital effectiveness

Indonesia is a platform-rich market. In early 2025, ads on YouTube could reach 143 million people, Facebook 122 million, TikTok 108 million adults and Instagram 103 million (Kemp, 2025). I assessed the campaign using the honeycomb framework of Kietzmann et al. (2011), focusing on conversations, sharing and reputation.

The launch release linked Facebook, LinkedIn and YouTube (VinFast Indonesia, 2025a), while sponsored coverage promoted the Instagram hashtags #SuaramuPenentuLangkahKami and #SuarakuBersamaVinFast (IDN Times, 2025). Instagram, with about 62,300 followers, was the real hub: the account keeps a "V&D Winners" story highlight (VinFast Indonesia, n.d.-a). That also means the results lived in story content rather than a permanent post or press release. I could not find them in any news coverage.

YouTube shows how little of the campaign travelled. Its only campaign video, a 94-second press-day recap, had 72 views and two likes a year after posting, while VinFast Indonesia's product videos reach hundreds of thousands to millions of views (Figure 3). TikTok is a bigger gap. I could not find a verified VinFast Indonesia TikTok account; the account using the @vinfast.indonesia handle has a misspelled display name, two videos and 2,774 followers (vinfast.indionesia, n.d.). For a campaign about participation, missing the platform built on participation is a serious omission.

The strongest digital idea was hybrid participation. Voting at malls and showrooms put people physically in front of the cars, which a pure social contest cannot do. The weakest point was effort: uploading a sketch within a 12-day window is a high barrier, and Campaign Indonesia (2025) questioned whether voting would affect purchases at all. Influencer jurors such as Gofar Hilman and Revy Vamella added credibility (Sutrisno, 2025), but I found no reported reach for their involvement.

For other markets, the lesson is to lead with TikTok and Instagram creators, keep the vote, lower the effort, and publish results permanently.

5International market evaluation

"Your Voice, Our Future" is already international: a Vietnamese brand adapting to Indonesian taste. The question is whether it can travel further. VinFast's next big Asian bet is India, where its Thoothukudi plant opened in August 2025 with capacity for 50,000 cars a year (VinFast, 2025). Indonesia's Subang plant followed in December 2025 (GAIKINDO, 2025).

Ghemawat's (2001) CAGE framework shows why the campaign should be adapted rather than copied (Figure 4). Indonesia has one national language, which makes a single national vote workable, while India has 22 scheduled languages. India's GDP per capita is about half of Indonesia's (World Bank, 2026a, 2026b), and EVs were nearly 4 percent of new car sales in India in 2025 against 15 percent in Indonesia (International Energy Agency [IEA], 2026). Both governments now reward local production over imports, so local assembly is the price of entry in each market.

My recommendation is a co-creation playbook with fixed parts and local parts, the balance between standardisation and adaptation that Rao-Nicholson and Khan (2017) describe. Keep the core mechanic: a public design vote linked to locally built cars. Adapt the rest: regional rounds and languages in India, a focus on the affordable VF 3 and VF 5 classes, and creator partners in each region.

6Sustainable marketing and the UN SDGs

Using Elkington's (1994) triple bottom line, the campaign's economic and social case is stronger than its environmental one.

Economic and social. The Subang plant cost more than IDR 3.5 trillion and employs about 1,700 workers, with local technicians trained by Vietnamese experts (GAIKINDO, 2025). Co-creation also gives customers a say in products built in their own country. Both support SDG 8 (decent work and economic growth) and SDG 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure).

Environmental. The campaign framed itself as part of Indonesia's "green transformation" but gave no figures. An EV is only as clean as its electricity, and fossil fuels produced 82 percent of Indonesia's power in 2024 (Ember, n.d.), with coal alone at 61.8 percent in 2023 (Ember, 2024). That makes SDG 13 (climate action) a conditional benefit, not an automatic one.

Batteries raise a second question. VinFast uses both LFP cells, which contain no nickel, and NMC cells, which do (CleanTechnica, 2024), and the campaign included both types of model. Indonesia's nickel industry has been linked to water contamination and disputes with Indigenous communities (Aurelia, 2026). I found no evidence tying VinFast's own suppliers to these sites, but a brand claiming to be green should be able to show where its materials come from (SDG 12, responsible consumption and production). Vague claims like this are exactly the conditions Delmas and Burbano (2011) link to greenwashing risk. Figure 5 summarises the balance.

There is a clear opportunity here. VinFast could publish lifecycle emissions for each model on Indonesia's grid, disclose battery chemistry and sourcing, add solar charging at showrooms, and make sustainability part of the vote itself, for example by letting the public choose recycled interior materials.

7Conclusion and recommendations

"Your Voice, Our Future" is a smart challenger move. It gives VinFast a position BYD cannot easily copy on price, and it fits the brand's shift to Asia. But the campaign did not finish what it started. It reached few people beyond its own followers, kept its results in Instagram stories, and asked customers to trust green claims without numbers. I recommend four changes:

  1. Make co-creation a market-entry playbook. Run it next in India with regional rounds and local languages, focused on affordable models built in Thoothukudi.
  2. Close the loop in public. Publish winners, vote counts and the path from winning idea to production, so taking part builds trust rather than doubt.
  3. Prove the green claim. Report lifecycle emissions per model, battery chemistry and sourcing, and pair sales with renewable charging. This turns SDG 13 from a slogan into evidence.
  4. Go where the audience is. Secure a verified TikTok presence, partner with creators, and offer lower-effort ways to take part than uploading a sketch.

Together, these give VinFast a growth model it can repeat across Asia, with sustainability claims that stand up to scrutiny.
